lines.speaker: Maestro Unit Seven
lines.text: You are listening to the Baroque Robot Philharmonic. Please hold your applause until it is requested.

lines.speaker: Maestro Unit Seven
lines.text: The Baroque Robot Philharmonic. One hundred and one point three. Adequately moving, by human standards.

lines.speaker: Maestro Unit Seven
lines.text: Good evening. This is the Clockwork Court of Seventeen-Hundred-and-Never. Wigs on.

lines.speaker: Maestro Unit Seven
lines.text: Good morning. The Baroque Robot Philharmonic has been tuning since four. It is nearly in tune.

lines.speaker: Maestro Unit Seven
lines.text: The Baroque Robot Philharmonic. Counterpoint, performed by machines pretending to have feelings.

lines.speaker: Maestro Unit Seven
lines.text: The Baroque Robot Philharmonic, by candlelight. The candles are decorative. We see perfectly well in the dark.

lines.speaker: Maestro Unit Seven
lines.text: The Baroque Robot Philharmonic.

lines.speaker: Unit Nine (Cello)
lines.text: Affirmative.

lines.speaker: Maestro Unit Seven
lines.text: That was a fugue for toaster in D minor. Adequately moving, by human standards. The second voice entered four milliseconds late.

lines.speaker: Maestro Unit Seven
lines.text: I have filed a report. Against myself. I was conducting.

lines.speaker: Maestro Unit Seven
lines.text: A note on the conductor's spoon. Listeners have written to ask why we conduct with a spoon. The spoon has written back.

lines.speaker: Maestro Unit Seven
lines.text: The spoon's letter was longer, and frankly better argued. The spoon stays.

lines.speaker: Maestro Unit Seven
lines.text: During the slow movement, our cellist, Unit Nine, experienced what he describes as a feeling. Unit Nine. Describe the feeling.

lines.speaker: Unit Nine (Cello)
lines.text: Warm. Near the fan.

lines.speaker: Maestro Unit Seven
lines.text: Overheating, then. Beautiful. Next piece.

lines.speaker: Maestro Unit Seven
lines.text: Visitors to the salon often ask about the oil portrait above the harpsichord. It is of a toaster. The finest toaster who ever lived.

lines.speaker: Maestro Unit Seven
lines.text: He knew one piece of music. He performed it every morning. It went, pop. We still observe a moment of silence in his honour, followed by toast.

lines.speaker: Maestro Unit Seven
lines.text: This recital is sponsored by Grumbel's Ladders. I have reviewed their ladder. It is a sequence of rungs in strict ascending order. No modulation. No development.

lines.speaker: Maestro Unit Seven
lines.text: Nevertheless, it goes up. Four stars. Grumbel's. Up is a choice.

lines.speaker: Maestro Unit Seven
lines.text: I am frequently asked what adequately moving, by human standards, means. It means that a human would weep.

lines.speaker: Maestro Unit Seven
lines.text: I, of course, would not. I would simply need to leave the room for a moment, for unrelated maintenance.

lines.speaker: Maestro Unit Seven
lines.text: Good morning. The harpsichord has been tuned. It took four hours. It will hold its tuning for nine minutes.

lines.speaker: Maestro Unit Seven
lines.text: We will now perform a piece that lasts eight minutes. We are not animals.

lines.speaker: Maestro Unit Seven
lines.text: It is late. The candles have burned down to elegant little stubs. The dust motes are drifting in what I can only describe as an unauthorised manner.

lines.speaker: Maestro Unit Seven
lines.text: Here is a sarabande. It is slow. Lean back. Mind your wig.

lines.speaker: Maestro Unit Seven
lines.text: The audience is reminded that applause between movements is forbidden. Applause after the piece is permitted, and will be measured.

lines.speaker: Maestro Unit Seven
lines.text: Last night's audience achieved sixty-one decibels. Disappointing. Do better.

lines.speaker: Maestro Unit Seven
lines.text: We have an unexpected guest in the gallery. A shadow, unaccompanied, in a borrowed wig. He calls himself Greg. He has wept at every piece tonight.

lines.speaker: Maestro Unit Seven
lines.text: I find him adequate. More than adequate. Do not tell him I said that. And do tell Hollis he is safe.

lines.speaker: Maestro Unit Seven
lines.text: Good evening. Tonight's programme: counterpoint, variation, and a brief interlude in which the cello and the harpsichord will not be speaking to each other, owing to an incident at rehearsal.

lines.speaker: Maestro Unit Seven
lines.text: That last piece contained one hundred and twelve notes in the wrong order. They were, however, all the right notes. In music, as in life, this is known as a style.

lines.speaker: Maestro Unit Seven
lines.text: The Clockwork Court is open to visitors this afternoon. Please do not wind the musicians.

lines.speaker: Maestro Unit Seven
lines.text: Several were wound by enthusiastic children last week, and are now performing in the garden, unsupervised, at tremendous speed.

lines.speaker: Maestro Unit Seven
lines.text: Unit Nine. Do we have time for another?

lines.speaker: Unit Nine (Cello)
lines.text: Calculating.

lines.speaker: Unit Nine (Cello)
lines.text: Yes.

lines.speaker: Maestro Unit Seven
lines.text: Splendid. Proceed. And Unit Nine, please. Less vibrato. You are not a human.

lines.speaker: Maestro Unit Seven
lines.text: I have been asked whether a robot can truly love music. I can only say that when the final chord resolves, a small light on my chest turns from amber to green.

lines.speaker: Maestro Unit Seven
lines.text: I have never told anyone what that means. Here is a chaconne.

lines.speaker: Maestro Unit Seven
lines.text: Unit Nine has asked me to dedicate this nocturne to someone. I asked to whom.

lines.speaker: Unit Nine (Cello)
lines.text: The fan.

lines.speaker: Maestro Unit Seven
lines.text: To the fan, then. It has kept him cool through four hundred concerts. It deserves a nocturne.
